questions.prompt: Why can a scheduler not always wait until it knows every operation in a transaction before choosing a schedule?
options: Applications may submit further queries while a transaction is running
Every transaction must declare all queries before BEGIN
Only COMMIT identifies the objects accessed
The lock manager can grant locks only after a query has finished
questions.explanation: The protocol must make decisions online because the complete query sequence may not yet have been submitted. A transaction cannot be assumed to contain just one query.

questions.prompt: T1 holds S-lock(A). Which request from T2 is compatible?
options: X-lock(A)
S-lock(A)
An immediate upgrade to X-lock(A) without waiting
An X-lock on all of A simply because T1 is reading
questions.explanation: Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks. An exclusive lock conflicts with another transaction's S-lock or X-lock; one transaction's read does not authorize concurrent writes.

questions.prompt: T1 holds X-lock(A). What must T2 do to read A under the lecture's locking scheme?
options: Read A, because S-locks are always compatible with X-locks
Acquire an X-lock alongside T1's X-lock
Wait until a compatible S-lock can be granted
Force T1 to downgrade immediately because reads have absolute priority
questions.explanation: A read requires an S-lock, which conflicts with T1's X-lock. T2 cannot bypass locking merely because its operation is a read.

questions.prompt: What does a lock manager normally do when a request conflicts with a currently held lock?
options: Grant it immediately and replace compatibility checks with undo
Permanently reject every transaction containing a read
Automatically downgrade the holder's X-lock without considering its transaction
Block the request until it can be granted or the transaction is otherwise handled
questions.explanation: The lock manager maintains a lock table and grants or blocks requests according to compatibility. It cannot make a conflicting request safe by arbitrarily downgrading a lock another transaction still needs.

questions.prompt: Is acquiring a lock before each access and releasing it whenever convenient enough to guarantee serializability?
options: No; a protocol such as 2PL is also needed
Yes, because each individual access is protected
Yes, if every transaction uses X-locks, however they are released
Yes, if the schedule contains only two transactions
questions.explanation: Protecting individual operations still permits nonserializable interleavings. Two-phase locking adds restrictions on when locks may be acquired and released.

questions.prompt: What may a transaction do in the growing phase of 2PL?
options: Release locks but acquire no new ones
Acquire new locks without releasing any
Acquire and release locks in any interleaved order
Read data but perform no writes
questions.explanation: The growing phase allows locks to accumulate. The first release begins the shrinking phase, ending the growing phase.

questions.prompt: T acquires S(A), acquires S(B), releases S(A), and then requests X(C). Where is 2PL violated?
options: When two S-locks are acquired
When S(A) is released after reading
When X(C) is requested after a lock has been released
When three different objects are accessed
questions.explanation: After the first release, 2PL forbids acquiring new locks. Neither the number of objects nor acquiring two shared locks is the problem.

questions.prompt: T holds S(A), releases a lock on B, and then upgrades S(A) to X(A). Does this follow 2PL?
options: Yes, because T already held a lock on A
Yes, because an upgrade is not a lock on a new object
Yes, as long as T has not committed, even after releasing another lock
No; upgrading after the shrinking phase begins violates 2PL
questions.explanation: Two-phase locking forbids both acquisition and upgrade after the growing phase. An existing S-lock does not permit a late upgrade.

questions.prompt: Which property does 2PL guarantee in the lecture?
options: Conflict serializability
Deadlocks can never occur
No schedule can read uncommitted data
Every transaction finishes without aborting
questions.explanation: Two-phase locking guarantees conflict-serializable schedules. Deadlocks and aborts can still occur, so the stronger absolute claims are false.

questions.prompt: Must every serializable schedule be allowed by 2PL?
options: Yes, because the two concepts are identical
No; 2PL is sufficient but more restrictive than the set of serializable schedules
Only if transactions write data
No serializable schedule can use 2PL
questions.explanation: Two-phase locking can reject a schedule that is nevertheless serializable. Guaranteeing safety does not mean permitting every safe schedule.

questions.prompt: T1 releases X(A) before finishing. T2 reads A as written by T1, and T1 then aborts. Why might T2 also have to abort?
options: T2 read only a committed value from T1
T2 merely started before T1 committed, without reading T1's data
T2 depended on an uncommitted value that is being withdrawn
Every transaction in the schedule must abort regardless of dependencies
questions.explanation: Cascading aborts propagate through dependencies on uncommitted data. They do not affect a transaction merely because it uses the same CPU or database system.

questions.prompt: Can basic 2PL release a lock before COMMIT?
options: No; every form of 2PL holds every lock until COMMIT
Only S-locks can be released; basic 2PL always retains every X-lock until the end
Yes, and it may then acquire any new locks before commit
Yes, during the shrinking phase
questions.explanation: Basic 2PL requires two phases but does not require all locks to remain until completion. Holding locks until the end is the strict variant used in this lecture.

questions.prompt: Does conflict serializability alone guarantee the absence of dirty reads?
options: No; serializability and handling uncommitted data are separate requirements
Yes; an acyclic graph forbids every read of uncommitted data
Yes, if there are only two transactions
No; every serializable schedule contains a dirty read
questions.explanation: Basic 2PL can produce a conflict-serializable schedule that still reads before the writer commits. These properties must not be treated as identical.

questions.prompt: T2 reads T1's uncommitted data and commits before T1 aborts. What makes this especially dangerous?
options: Only T1 needs undoing; T2's committed result is always valid
T2 has published a result that depends on a failed transaction
T2's commit automatically commits T1's data
Reordering the COMMIT statements on paper repairs all effects
questions.explanation: T2's published result cannot be assumed valid after its source data is undone. T2's COMMIT does not repair the invalid dependency.

questions.prompt: Which method in the lecture prevents cascading aborts caused by reading uncommitted data?
options: Release X-locks immediately after writes
Keep every S-lock but always release X-locks before commit
Use strict 2PL and hold locks until transaction completion
Require only an acyclic conflict graph, without considering commits
questions.explanation: Retaining X-locks prevents other transactions from reading temporary values. Releasing them early creates the very dependency that can cause a cascade.

questions.prompt: Under this lecture's strict-2PL convention, when are locks released?
options: Immediately after each read or write
As soon as the last lock has been acquired, even if work continues
As soon as another transaction requests them and waits
At the end of the transaction
questions.explanation: The lecture's diagram retains all locks until transaction completion. Some sources call this convention rigorous 2PL, so use the explicitly stated definition.

questions.prompt: T1 transfers 6 units between A and B while T2 computes their total. What does holding both locks until T1 finishes achieve?
options: T2 cannot observe a partially completed transfer
T2 is guaranteed to run before T1
Every SUM can run without S-locks
Every deadlock is automatically eliminated
questions.explanation: T2 can read only after the required compatible locks are available. This does not force T2 to run first, and deadlocks with other transactions remain possible.

questions.prompt: T1 aborts while holding X(A) until completion. Why is undo generally simpler than after releasing the lock early?
options: The lock stores the before-image and replaces the log
No other transaction has overwritten A through T1's lock
Aborted transactions never need data-page restoration
Keeping a lock automatically makes every data page NO-STEAL
questions.explanation: Retaining the X-lock protects the object during rollback. The lock itself does not replace the log or other recovery information.

questions.prompt: Does strict 2PL prevent T1 from holding A while waiting for B and T2 from holding B while waiting for A?
options: Yes; keeping locks longer eliminates every waiting cycle
Yes, if both transactions use X-locks
No; deadlock is still possible
No, because strict 2PL does not guarantee serializability
questions.explanation: Strictness prevents dependencies on uncommitted data but does not itself solve deadlock. Strict 2PL still guarantees conflict serializability.

questions.prompt: Which sequence follows the lecture's strict-2PL convention?
options: Acquire X(A), write, release it, then acquire X(B)
Acquire S(A), read, release it, and continue until commit
Acquire X(A), write, and release it before commit so others can read temporary data
Acquire S(A), acquire X(B), perform the work, commit, and release both locks
questions.explanation: Retaining the locks until completion matches the lecture's convention. Early release of S-locks may fit another definition of strictness, but it does not fit this one.

questions.prompt: When does a waits-for graph contain T1→T2?
options: T1 is waiting for a lock held by T2
T1 committed before T2
T1 reads the same table as T2 without waiting
T1 has an earlier timestamp than T2, regardless of locks
questions.explanation: A waits-for edge represents a current wait. A precedence edge instead represents the order of conflicting operations that have occurred.

questions.prompt: T1 holds X(A) and waits for B; T2 holds X(B) and waits for A. What does the waits-for graph contain?
options: Only T1→T2
The cycle T1→T2→T1
No edges, because each lock has only one holder
Only an A→B edge between objects
questions.explanation: Each transaction waits for the other, producing two edges between transaction vertices. The graph's vertices are not the objects A and B.

questions.prompt: How does the lecture break a deadlock once it is detected?
options: Grant an X-lock even though its current holder has not released it
Change priorities while leaving the waiting cycle intact
Select a victim, roll it back, and release its locks
Wait until all transactions in the cycle commit on their own
questions.explanation: Aborting a victim breaks at least one waiting dependency. Ignoring lock compatibility would sacrifice correctness.

questions.prompt: Why consider the number of previous restarts when choosing a deadlock victim?
options: To make the newest transaction always win regardless of cost
To preferentially abort the same victim on every retry
To ignore the locks already held by a transaction
To avoid repeatedly aborting one transaction and starving it
questions.explanation: Victim selection should avoid repeatedly penalizing the same transaction. Restart counts help with fairness; they do not replace recovery or query processing.

questions.prompt: What is the trade-off in checking for deadlocks more frequently?
options: Earlier detection requires more checking overhead
More frequent checks always reduce CPU cost
Cycles are guaranteed never to form
Victim selection is no longer needed when a cycle exists
questions.explanation: Detection reacts to cycles and has a computational cost. Frequent checking is not the same as preventing every deadlock.

questions.prompt: Under wait-die, an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger transaction. What happens?
options: The older transaction immediately aborts
The older transaction waits
The younger transaction is immediately aborted
Both transactions hold the X-lock
questions.explanation: Wait-die lets an older requester wait for a younger holder. Only a younger requester facing an older holder aborts; do not confuse this with wound-wait.

questions.prompt: Under wait-die, a younger transaction requests a lock held by an older transaction. What happens?
options: The older transaction aborts
The younger transaction always waits
The younger transaction aborts
The older transaction releases its lock without rollback
questions.explanation: The younger requester must die. Allowing it to wait would violate wait-die's permitted direction of waiting.

questions.prompt: Under wound-wait, an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger transaction. What happens?
options: The older transaction always waits
The older transaction aborts
Both wait for one another without choosing a victim
The younger lock holder is aborted
questions.explanation: In wound-wait, the older transaction wounds the younger one. This differs from wait-die, where the older requester waits.

questions.prompt: Under wound-wait, a younger transaction requests a lock held by an older transaction. What happens?
options: The younger transaction waits
The younger transaction aborts the older one
The older transaction must always abort
Both abort regardless of age
questions.explanation: Wound-wait allows younger transactions to wait for older ones. A younger requester cannot wound an older holder.

questions.prompt: Why retain a transaction's original timestamp when it restarts?
options: To make it the youngest transaction after every retry
To preserve its age priority and reduce starvation across retries
To allow waiting edges to reverse direction freely after restart
To let it ignore lock compatibility after its first abort
questions.explanation: Assigning a fresh timestamp on every retry could leave a transaction perpetually young and disadvantaged. Keeping its timestamp preserves the protocol's age-based priority.
